topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Geometric View of a Matrix
sections.content: Define a matrix not just as a grid of numbers, but as a function. A matrix A transforms a vector v into a new vector Av. Visualize this as a transformation of the 2D plane (e.g., rotation, scaling, or shearing).
sections.example: Visualize a 2x2 matrix transforming the unit square (defined by vectors i and j) into a parallelogram.

sections.title: Defining Composition: One Step After Another
sections.content: Introduce the concept of applying two transformations sequentially. If transformation A is applied first, then B is applied to the result, we denote this as B(Av).
sections.example: Imagine a cat icon on a grid: First, matrix A rotates the cat 90 degrees; then, matrix B doubles its size. The final position is the result of applying B(A(v)).

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: Matrix Multiplication
sections.content: Explain that matrix multiplication (BA) is defined precisely to represent this composition. The columns of the new matrix BA are the results of applying the second transformation B to the columns of the first transformation A.
sections.example: Show the calculation steps clearly: The result of applying B to the transformed basis vectors of A creates the columns of the new matrix BA.

sections.title: Visual Synthesis: The Sequential Path
sections.content: Animate the 'Path of a Vector': A vector v moves under A, then the resulting vector moves under B. Show that the single matrix BA achieves this movement in one jump.
sections.example: A robotic arm movement: Matrix A shifts the arm segment, and Matrix B adjusts the gripper. Show that multiplying the matrices creates a single 'master' transformation that tracks the final state instantly.

sections.title: Closing: Why Order Matters
sections.content: Conclude by highlighting non-commutativity (AB ≠ BA). Use the physical intuition: rotating then scaling a shape is often different from scaling then rotating it.
sections.example: Use a character (e.g., a 'Game Sprite') to show that rotating 90° then stretching vertically results in a different final pose than stretching then rotating.
